claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an fcc matrix.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by the formation and stability of a fine-grained oxide scale.
An oxidizing atmosphere rapidly produces a continuous Al- and Cr-enriched oxide barrier.
The continuous Al- and Cr-enriched oxide barrier limits oxygen ingress and internal oxidation.
Under reducing conditions, the oxide barrier is less effective and consequently permits more internal oxidation and degradation.
The as-built alloy has a homogeneous fcc microstructure.
The as-built alloy is known for high strength and fatigue resistance.
The as-built alloy has no preexisting oxide scale.
The relevant structural mediator is a continuous, fine-grained oxide scale enriched in Al and Cr.
Ti may contribute to formation of a spinel-type oxide structure.
The oxide scale mediates oxygen transport into the fcc matrix.
In oxidizing environments, an adherent, slow-growing oxide scale protects the matrix by limiting further oxygen ingress.
In reducing atmospheres, an incomplete or destabilized oxide scale accelerates microstructural degradation by failing to prevent internal oxidation.
The alloy retains enough fcc integrity under reducing exposure to support high strength and fatigue performance up to an unspecified threshold.
Oxidizing exposure at about 800°C for 200 hours will produce a thin, continuous scale, minimal internal degradation, and preserved mechanical properties.
Reducing exposure at about 800°C for 200 hours will produce a less uniform or thinner scale, more subsurface oxide precipitation, and greater mechanical-property loss than oxidizing exposure.
At substantially higher temperatures or much longer durations, creep or phase transformations may dominate over oxide-scale-controlled degradation.
Prior studies in simpler alloy systems support protective oxide formation by Al and Cr.
The respective contributions of Ti and multielement synergistic or antagonistic interactions to scale formation remain uncertain.

Similar oxide scales and internal-oxidation profiles in both atmospheres, or absence of correlation between scale integrity and mechanical degradation, would falsify oxide-scale control of degradation.
